title: Why Do You Forget Why You Entered a Room?
hook: You walk into the kitchen. And completely forget why.

segments.n: You walk into the kitchen. And completely forget why. You’re not losing your mind. It has a name.

segments.n: It’s called the doorway effect. In one study, people forgot more after crossing a doorway than after walking the same distance inside one room.
segments.p: Split scene: on the left Hiro walking across one big room leaving a short trail of dots, on the right Hiro stepping through a doorway into another room, the doorway frame colored amber-orange, a tiny thought bubble floating away above him. segments.n: Researchers think your brain treats a doorway like the end of a scene, and files the old thoughts away.
segments.p: Hiro standing beside a doorway, a small filing cabinet next to him with a thought bubble being slid into a drawer, the drawer colored amber-orange, plain pale background. segments.n: Think of a movie. When the scene changes, the last scene fades out. Your mind does something similar with rooms.
segments.p: A movie theater screen showing two simple scenes side by side, the left scene fading with dotted lines, the right scene sharp, a clapperboard colored amber-orange, Hiro seated in front watching with a popcorn bucket. segments.n: So what helps? Go back to the room where you had the thought. The place itself can bring it back.
segments.p: Hiro walking back into the first room, a light bulb above his head colored amber-orange, a table with a notebook in the background. segments.n: Try saying your goal out loud before you move. It’s not a flaw. It’s your brain turning the page. What did you forget today?
